Four Pedal Circles

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Four circles drawn from one point and four corners all pass through the same dot; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag A, B, C, D or P, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, pedal triangles and perpendicular lines.

Drag a point, or focus it and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

A complete quadrangle is four points and all six lines between them. Take any three points and you get a triangle. From a fifth point P you can drop three perpendiculars to that triangle's sides: the three feet form a pedal triangle, and its circumcircle is the pedal circle. The surprising thing is what the four pedal circles do.

One point for all four circles

The page claims that the four pedal circles defined by a point and a complete quadrangle are concurrent: they all pass through one point Q. The logic test checked 1,500 non-degenerate configurations with an independent circumcircle formula, and the largest distance from Q to any of the four circles was below 0.0001. Each pair of circles shares one pedal foot — circles ABC and ABD both go through the foot on AB, while ACD and BCD share the foot on CD. Their other intersections are the same point Q, so the applet averages those two answers.

A small quirk in the applet

To pick the "other" intersection, the original code keeps the one at least 1 unit from the shared foot. If the two intersections sit closer than that, it can pick the foot by mistake and draw Q a little away from the true meeting point. This port keeps that behaviour, so the picture follows the applet. The theorem itself does not depend on the choice: the test used the textbook circle intersection and found the four circles concurrent in every well-conditioned case tested. When the three feet nearly line up, the applet even draws a straight Simson line in place of that circle.

When the four points lie on a circle

The page adds that for a cyclic quadrangle the four Simson lines — each corner with respect to the triangle of the other three — and the four nine-point circles all meet in one point. Across 700 cyclic quadrangles the test found the three feet of each Simson line collinear, the four lines concurrent, and the same point on every nine-point circle (largest error below 0.0001).

A fact for every quadrangle

The last claim on the page generalises this: for any four points, the nine-point circles of BCD, CDA, DAB and ABC and the pedal circles of the remaining point A, B, C and D are concurrent. The test found a common point on all eight circles in hundreds of quadrangles, with error below 0.0001. The page ends with "to be continued"; no further formula is stated there.

Try dragging P close to one of the four corners: its three feet almost line up and the pedal circle flattens into a line. Then tick Pedal triangles and Perpendiculars to see where the circles come from.
